Complementary information — Evidence spans routine blood tests, liquid biopsy, and specialized multi-cancer tests, each addressing different roles and limitations in cancer detection

Routine blood tests are generally not stand-alone diagnostic tools for most cancers, but they can provide supportive clues about organ function and abnormal chemicals or proteins that may indicate cancer, and are often used alongside other tests [d1]. Routine blood work can detect early signs of cancers, particularly blood cancers such as leukemia and lymphoma, and may offer insight into organ function and potential cancer indicators [d2]. A blood-based “liquid biopsy” can detect circulating tumor DNA and help identify specific genetic changes, though it cannot diagnose cancer itself [d3]. In lymphoma follow-up, routine blood tests have limited utility: they detected relapse in only about 5% of relapsed patients, with sensitivity around 42% and a positive predictive value near 9% [d4,d8]. Routine blood tests may show elevated liver enzymes suggestive of possible liver metastasis, but results are often normal even when advanced cancer is present [d5]. Specialized multi-cancer early detection blood tests (e.g., Galleri) can detect cancer signals across more than 50 cancer types in adults at elevated risk, but are not routine blood tests and require confirmatory diagnostic evaluation [d6]. For skin cancer, routine blood tests and imaging scans are not used as screening tools, though research is exploring blood-based detection of skin cancer DNA [d7].
